name: Quitting smoking / vaping

lead: Smokers tend to show a characteristic aged look called smoker's face, with a distinctive wrinkle pattern and sallow grey skin. Some people quit to slow premature aging and look younger.

Smoking raises collagen- and elastin-degrading enzymes, narrows blood vessels and increases oxidative stress. A 1985 BMJ study reported certain facial features in about 46% of continuing smokers and 8% of former smokers who had smoked for a decade, and observational data show the features are less common in former smokers. How much reverses after quitting is not well established, and the sources reviewed do not address vaping and skin.

paras: People quit by going cold turkey, tapering, or using nicotine replacement and cessation programmes, and track their skin tone and wrinkles over months. Medical support is available for those who need it.

Smoking carries major documented harms including cancers, heart and lung disease, and quitting is associated with falling lung cancer risk over years. Nicotine withdrawal causes irritability and cravings for a period.

angle.text: Appearance communities cite quitting to slow premature skin aging, since smoking degrades collagen, narrows blood vessels and leaves a wrinkled, sallow smoker's face. The face is well documented; observational data show it is less common in former smokers, though reversal is thinly studied.

lead: Quitting smoking or vaping is a practice appearance communities associate with healthier-looking, younger-looking skin and a leaner, fresher look. The face of long-term smokers has a documented pattern, often called smoker's face, that includes a characteristic wrinkle pattern, sagging and a sallow grey skin tone, and people who quit do so partly with the aim of avoiding or slowing these changes.[1]

A 1985 BMJ study by D. Model reported certain facial features in about 46% of continuing smokers but only about 8% of former smokers who had smoked for a decade.[1] Proposed mechanisms include raised matrix metalloproteinases that break down collagen and elastin, narrowed blood vessels that cut oxygen delivery to skin, and oxidative stress.[1] Research on vaping has concentrated on lung and cardiovascular effects rather than skin.[2][3][4]

On looksmaxxing forums, the topic runs in two directions. Some members describe nicotine from vapes as an appetite suppressant and leanmaxxing tool, while others describe quitting as part of a routine to improve skin, stamina and general condition. Reported experiences are anecdotal.[5][6][7]

paras: Smoking is classed as an extrinsic aging factor. It lowers oxygen delivery to skin, depletes antioxidants such as vitamin C and raises enzymes that break down the structural matrix of the skin, leaving it thinner and more lax.[1] Wikipedia also lists hair loss, gum disease, tooth staining and a higher skin cancer risk among smoking-associated changes.[1]

sections.h: What quitting is reported to change
paras: In the 1985 BMJ study described on Wikipedia, the facial features occurred in about 46% of continuing smokers and 8% of former smokers with a ten-year history, and were absent in non-smoking controls.[1] That comparison is observational; the sources do not state how fast or how completely skin recovers after stopping.

Lung cancer risk is reported to begin falling soon after quitting and to drop by about half after ten years.[8] A T Nation member in a long-running quit thread described being a week in and noticing that his skin had color and breathing was easier.[9]

Vaping is often described by users as a way to stop smoking or to curb appetite. Reviews in medical journals say vaping is not without risk, and that the e-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) outbreak of 2019 led to more than 2,800 hospitalizations in the United States.[2][3][4] An American Heart Association scientific statement says cardiovascular and pulmonary effects of long-term use remain under study.[4][10] No study found has measured facial skin changes after stopping vaping.
Randomized trials have tested ways of helping young people stop vaping, including a text-message program for adolescents and a trial of varenicline with counseling in youth who vape.[11][12]

On looksmax.org, threads describe nicotine vaping as an appetite suppressant for cutting weight, with posters writing about leaner faces; other members answer that it irritates their lungs or may affect growth, and some threads record quitting attempts.[5][6][13] A thread asks whether quitting smoking helps rebuild collagen.[14]

No studies found on quitting vaping for appearance. For smoking, one observational study compared facial features of current, former and non-smokers.[1] Randomized trials of vaping cessation measure quitting rates rather than skin outcomes.[11][12]

lore.intro: Looksmaxxing forums discuss nicotine in two ways: as a leanmaxxing aid and as something to quit for skin, lungs and stamina.[5][6]
